traveler: Bathyllus of Alexandria (Bathyllus Alexandrinus), freedman of Maecenas
title: The Byname and the Silent Body: an Alexandrian Dancer in the House of Maecenas
years: fl. c. 23 BCE to after 8 BCE; birth and death unrecorded
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Byname and the Great Harbour

stops.name: Alexandria, the only word the record keeps
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No ancient source gives a birth year; mid-first-century BCE is a modern estimate back-projected from his Augustan floruit. Athenaeus supplies the byname Alexandreus and nothing further: no parents, no quarter, no date.
stops.campa: Of everything a life ordinarily leaves behind, this one keeps a single adjective: Alexandrian. Athenaeus calls him Bathyllus ho Alexandreus, and every later hand copies the word without adding to it. No father is named, no mother, no street, no year. The city itself is the whole of his documented origin: Greek-speaking, Ptolemaic, packed with theatres and festival processions and the machinery of royal spectacle. He is a boy somewhere in it, in the last decades before Rome takes the city. Athenaeus was writing around the year 200, two centuries after the fact.
suggested_refs: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d-f, the fullest ancient notice of Bathyllus
The testimonia collection at theatrum.de, s.v. Bathyllus I

stops.name: Alexandria, the Mouseion quarter and an unnamed teacher
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction throughout. No source names a teacher, a school, a company, or any Alexandrian performance. The formation is inferred backward from what his mature art demanded, and the date is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: In the Bruchion, where the Mouseion and the Library stand and the Ptolemies pay for scholars and processions out of the same purse, dance is a trade with masters and pupils. Nobody records his. Not one surviving sentence gives Bathyllus a teacher, a troupe, or a first performance in Egypt. What that silence has to cover is considerable: command of masks, of the tempo of pipes, of the hand-language the Greeks call cheironomia, and of three separate dance idioms he will later be said to have fused. Somewhere in this quarter a man taught a boy all of it and left no name.
suggested_refs: Marie-Helene Garelli, Danser le mythe (2007), on the Hellenistic background of Roman pantomime
Ismene Lada-Richards, Silent Eloquence (2007)
sources: Absence of any named teacher across Athenaeus, Seneca the Elder, Crinagoras, Persius, Phaedrus
Colegio Invisible research pass, formation section

stops.name: Alexandria, the sentence in Athenaeus that will not sit still
stops.date_confidence: Ordering date only, assigned to place a textual problem at his city of origin. Athenaeus wrote c. 200 CE; the crux belongs to the transmitted text, not to anything in Bathyllus's life. The reading of 'Memphis' as a place rather than a nickname is not resolved here.
stops.campa: The passage that preserves him also confuses him. Athenaeus at 1.20d writes that the first to introduce this tragic dancing, as it was called, in the style of Memphis, was Bathyllus of Alexandria. A few lines earlier he has been discussing a performer nicknamed Memphis, whose body was said to move like the city itself. Readers have taken the phrase for Egyptian temple dance and built an apprenticeship on it. The same passage calls Bathyllus's manner the jollier of the two styles, which is not what tragic means. Two claims, one sentence, no way to make them agree.
suggested_refs: Athenaeus 1.20c-d on the dancer nicknamed Memphis, immediately preceding the Bathyllus notice

stops.name: Alexandria, the Great Harbour and a crossing nobody wrote down
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No source narrates the voyage, its date, its route, or whether he crossed already enslaved or was bought after landing. Only the sequence, Alexandria first and Rome after, is attested.
stops.campa: The grain ships load at the Eastern Harbour under the Pharos and run for Italy on the summer winds. At some unrecorded year Bathyllus is on one of them. Whether he goes as a hired performer and is sold later, or crosses already as the property of a Roman buyer, no text says. The tradition preserves only that he began in Alexandria and ended famous in Rome, and leaves everything between them blank. He is young enough that the whole career is still ahead of him and skilled enough to be worth the freight. The ships clear the Pharos on the north-west wind and are in open water for a fortnight or more.
suggested_refs: The Alexandria-to-Puteoli grain corridor of the late Republic and early Empire
sources: Inference from the biographical sequence common to all ancient testimonia; no source narrates the voyage

segments.name: Bought Into the House on the Esquiline

stops.name: Puteoli, the ordinary landfall
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, route inference only. No source places Bathyllus at Puteoli or names any port of entry. It stands here as the standard Alexandria-to-Italy landfall of the period, the corridor Seneca the Younger later describes for the Alexandrian fleet.
stops.campa: Everything that comes out of Egypt comes ashore here first: grain, glass, linen, papyrus, people. The Alexandrian fleet is recognisable from the mole before it docks, its topsails set where other ships strike them, and the whole bay turns out to watch it come in. If Bathyllus travels the normal route, this is where Italy begins for him, in a harbour that speaks as much Greek as Latin and has been receiving Alexandrians for a century and a half. No ancient writer says he was ever here. The corridor is attested; the man on it is not.
suggested_refs: Seneca the Younger, Epistulae 77.1, on the arrival of the Alexandrian fleet at Puteoli
sources: General pattern of Alexandria-Puteoli shipping in the period; no source names Bathyllus's port of entry

stops.name: Porta Capena, into the city by the Appian Way
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, route inference only. No text records his arrival in Rome, by any gate, in any year, or in any company.
stops.campa: A dancer arriving from Alexandria in these years arrives into a capital that is rebuilding itself and has decided it wants spectacle. Past the gate the city is still mostly brick and timber: one stone theatre, twenty-odd years old, the civil wars barely finished, Actium only three years back. The road up from Campania comes through the Alban hills and enters Rome under the arch where the aqueduct leaks on everyone passing beneath it, which is why the poets keep calling that gate wet.
suggested_refs: The Porta Capena and the head of the Via Appia inside Augustan Rome
sources: Standard topography of arrival routes into Augustan Rome from the south; not attested for Bathyllus individually

stops.name: The Esquiline, the household of Maecenas
stops.date_confidence: Attested that he belonged to Gaius Cilnius Maecenas as slave and later freedman, this being the tradition standing behind Tacitus and Cassius Dio; no date survives for the acquisition. Pin follows the traditional Largo Leopardi identification of the horti. T. P. Wiseman, PBSR 84 (2016), argues the gardens lay instead on the eastern slope of the mons Oppius, and that dispute is recorded here rather than settled.
stops.campa: Gaius Cilnius Maecenas handles for Octavian everything that is not war, and keeps on the Esquiline a house of gardens, music, and private theatricals where the regime's poets are fed and read aloud to each other. Virgil comes into this circle; so does Horace. Bathyllus comes into it as property. The same rooms that hear the Georgics rehearsed hold a young Alexandrian who can be bought or lent out at his owner's word. Wiseman argues there was a theatre inside the gardens, and puts the gardens themselves on the eastern slope of the Oppian, not where the traditional identification has them.
suggested_refs: T. P. Wiseman, 'Maecenas and the Stage,' Papers of the British School at Rome 84 (2016), 131-155, arguing for a private theatre in the horti
sources: Wiseman, PBSR 84 (2016), describing Bathyllus as Maecenas's slave, freedman and lover

stops.name: The Esquiline, freed without a document
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to date and form. That he was manumitted is a secure inference from later sources calling him Maecenas's freedman; no manumission record, year, ceremony, or citizen name survives. The name Gaius Cilnius Bathyllus is a modern extrapolation from naming convention and appears in no ancient text.
stops.campa: At some point the ownership ends and the patronage begins. Roman law has a shape for this: the rod laid on the shoulder, the praetor's word, the freedman taking his patron's praenomen and nomen and keeping his slave name last. By that convention he walks out of the ceremony as Gaius Cilnius Bathyllus. No inscription, no letter, and no historian ever gives him that name, and the moderns who supply it are supplying it. What changes in law does not change in the house. He stays where he was, and the man who owned him now owes him bread and protection.
suggested_refs: Roman manumission naming convention, freedman praenomen and nomen from the patron
sources: Modern scholarly inference from manumission convention; no ancient text gives the citizen name
theatrum.de, s.v. Bathyllus I, on the slave-then-freedman sequence

stops.name: The Esquiline, effuso in amorem Bathylli
stops.date_confidence: Attested but late and undated. Tacitus wrote under Trajan or Hadrian, roughly 130 years after the Augustan period he is describing, and gives no date, no age for Bathyllus, and no account of consent. Cassius Dio, a century later still, is the only corroboration.
stops.campa: Tacitus, explaining a century afterward why Augustus tolerated the theatre at all, gives the reason in a subordinate clause: the emperor was humouring Maecenas, who had poured himself out in love of Bathyllus. Cassius Dio says the same thing in Greek and calls the dancer Maecenas's favourite. Two historians, neither of them contemporary, agree on the fact and record nothing around it. Not when it began, not whether it outlasted the manumission, not what a slave in that household was in a position to refuse. An imperial policy on public entertainment is explained by an appetite, and the appetite's object gets no line of his own.
stops.quote: indulserat ei ludicro Augustus, dum Maecenati obtemperat effuso in amorem Bathylli
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 1.54, in the account of the first Augustal Games of 14 CE
sources: Tacitus, Annals 1.54 (penelope.uchicago.edu, Loeb; Latin at thelatinlibrary.com)

stops.name: The Theatre of Pompey, the only stone theatre standing
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to venue. No ancient source names where Bathyllus performed. Pompey's theatre, dedicated 55 BCE, was Rome's only permanent stone theatre until Marcellus's was completed in 13 BCE and inaugurated in 12; the inference rests on building chronology alone.
stops.campa: Rome has one permanent theatre in these years, Pompey's, on the Campus Martius, with the temple of Venus Victrix set at the head of the seats so that the whole structure can be called a shrine with steps. Everything else is timber, raised for a festival and pulled down after. Into this single stone bowl comes a form the city has not seen organised before: one masked dancer, silent, taking every role in a story while others sing and pipe it behind him. Within a season the crowd has learned to read a plot off a pair of hands.
suggested_refs: The Theatre of Pompey, dedicated 55 BCE, and its temple of Venus Victrix
sources: Theatre-building chronology of Augustan Rome; venue not stated in any source naming Bathyllus

stops.name: The Theatre of Pompey, three Greek dances made into one Roman one
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Athenaeus 1.20e on the authority of Aristonicus, an antiquarian of uncertain date, who credits the synthesis to Bathyllus and Pylades jointly. The venue and the year are this pass's ordering inference and are not in the source.
stops.campa: Aristonicus, quoted by Athenaeus, sets down what the two of them did. Out of the comic fling called the cordax, the tragic measures called emmeleia, and the satyr rout called sicinnis, Bathyllus together with Pylades made the Italian style of dance. Three Greek genres, each with its own tempo and its own indecencies, collapsed into one vocabulary a Roman audience could follow without a Greek education. Pylades writes a treatise about it, the Peri orcheseos, now lost. Aristonicus, an antiquarian of unknown date quoted by Athenaeus two centuries later, is the only authority for any of it.
stops.quote: Aristonicus says that this Bathyllus, together with Pylades, who wrote a treatise on dancing, developed the Italian style of dance out of the comic fling called the cordax, the tragic measures called emmeleia, and the satyr rout called sicinnis.
suggested_refs: The lost Peri orcheseos of Pylades, attributed to him by Athenaeus
E. J. Jory, 'The Literary Evidence for the Beginnings of Imperial Pantomime,' BICS 28 (1981)
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e (penelope.uchicago.edu), citing Seleucus and Aristonicus

stops.name: Rome, the singer taken off the dancer's back
stops.date_confidence: The Jerome entry is attested (Chronicle, Ol. 189.3 = Abr. 1995 = 22 BCE) but credits Pylades alone. The year therefore dates the emergence of the reformed form, not anything documented about Bathyllus himself; only Athenaeus's separate tradition joins the two men as co-organisers. Modern reconstructions that prefer 23 BCE and the funeral games for Marcellus are not reconciled with Jerome here.
stops.campa: Jerome's Latin continuation of Eusebius fixes the technical reform to a year: in 22 BCE the dancer stops singing his own part. A chorus and pipes carry the words, and the body carries everything else. Jerome credits Pylades and does not mention Bathyllus, so the date belongs to the form rather than to the man. From now on the dancer's whole instrument is the body, and the words belong to men standing behind him. Whether Bathyllus took up the reform in that same year, or later, or had been working that way already, Jerome does not say.
suggested_refs: Jerome, Chronicle, entry at Ol. 189.3 / Abr. 1995 (22 BCE), on Pylades and the separation of song from dance
sources: Jerome's continuation of Eusebius, Chronicle, under 22 BCE
Jory (1981) on the literary evidence for the beginnings of imperial pantomime

stops.name: Rome, Crinagoras writes to Philonides
stops.date_confidence: Attested but undated. Crinagoras of Mytilene is an Augustan contemporary, which makes this the only surviving text written in Bathyllus's own lifetime that shows him working; nothing fixes the year within the reign, and the epigram names no venue. The year here orders the segment.
stops.campa: Crinagoras of Mytilene, a Greek epigrammatist attached to the imperial house, writes to the singer Philonides telling him to set a piece for four parts or even more. It is a note between colleagues about a production still in preparation: a libretto, a voice, and a dancer who will carry four characters or more without saying a word, all of it planned in advance. Crinagoras is an Augustan contemporary, which makes this the only text composed in Bathyllus's lifetime that shows him working. Neither your singing, he promises, nor the motions of Bathyllus's hands will want for grace.
stops.quote: Neither your singing nor the motions of Bathyllus' hands shall be lacking in grace.
stops.quote_source: Crinagoras of Mytilene, Greek Anthology 9.542, W. R. Paton's translation lightly revised (attalus.org)
suggested_refs: Crinagoras, Greek Anthology 9.542 (Gow-Page 39), Greek text at anthologiagraeca.org
sources: Crinagoras of Mytilene, Greek Anthology 9.542 (attalus.org, modernised Paton)

stops.name: The Circus Flaminius quarter, the Satyr
stops.date_confidence: The routine is attested only through Persius, writing c. 60-62 CE, some eighty years after the 22 BCE horizon. That it belonged to Bathyllus's own repertoire rather than his school's is the natural reading but is not stated. The date orders the segment and documents nothing.
stops.campa: One piece of his choreography keeps its name for eighty years after him: the Satyr of Bathyllus, a satyric solo famous enough that Persius can use three of its beats as a measure of what an amateur thinks he has mastered. Not one step of it is described in any surviving text. In all else a ditch-digger, the satirist says, and yet you move through three counts of Bathyllus's Satyr and call yourself a free man. The joke only works if the routine is known to everyone in the room and hard enough that partial knowledge of it is funny.
stops.quote: tris tantum ad numeros Satyrum moveare Bathylli
suggested_refs: Persius, Satires 5.122-124, in A. S. Kline's translation at poetryintranslation.com
sources: Persius, Satires 5.123 (thelatinlibrary.com); English at poetryintranslation.com, trans. A. S. Kline

stops.name: Rome, the register he was weaker in
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3 praef. 10, written under Tiberius and recalling the Augustan stage. The genre assignment is a real crux and is left open here: the Athenaeus passage that calls Bathyllus's manner the jollier also credits him with introducing tragic dancing to Rome.
stops.campa: Seneca the Elder, arguing that specialists come apart outside their specialty, reaches for the two dancers: Pylades in comedy, Bathyllus in tragedy stray far from themselves. The sentence assigns comedy to Bathyllus and tragedy to Pylades, and it also records that Bathyllus did take tragic roles and was judged inferior in them. Athenaeus meanwhile says the man introduced tragic dancing to Rome and calls his manner the more cheerful of the two. The tidy comic-against-tragic division that later scholarship draws around these names rests on one preface, and it does not survive contact with the other source.
stops.quote: Pylades in comoedia, Bathyllus in tragoedia multum a se aberrant.
stops.quote_source: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3, praefatio 10 (Latin, thelatinlibrary.com)
suggested_refs: Athenaeus 1.20d, on Bathyllus introducing 'tragic dancing' while dancing in the jollier manner

segments.name: The Rivalry That Divided the Audience

stops.name: Rome, Pylades of Cilicia
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the two were rivals and joint founders of the form (Athenaeus, both Senecas, Cassius Dio). No source dates the beginning of the rivalry or describes a first meeting. The year here orders the segment.
stops.campa: Pylades of Cilicia is the other half of the invention and the whole of the difficulty. A freedman too, a foreigner too, brought into the same new spectacle economy, he takes the grand and passionate register while Bathyllus takes the lighter one, and the audience divides between them. Ancient writers almost never name one without the other: Seneca the Elder uses them as a matched pair, Seneca the Younger names their two houses in a single breath, Athenaeus credits them jointly with making the Italian dance. Pylades is the one who wrote the book, and the one the emperor exiled.
suggested_refs: The lost treatise Peri orcheseos of Pylades, the only book either dancer is said to have written

stops.name: The Palatine, Augustus rebukes the wrong man
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Cassius Dio 54.17.4-5, which falls under 18 BCE in Book 54's consular sequence; Dio wrote c. 220-230 CE, some two and a half centuries later. The site is not named in the source, and the Palatine stands in as Augustus's habitual seat.
stops.campa: Dio sets the order of events out plainly. Pylades has been exiled for stirring up sedition and then brought back by the emperor himself. Restored, he quarrels with Bathyllus, and Augustus reprimands him for it. Pylades answers that it is to Caesar's advantage for the people to spend their idle hours on the two of them. The princeps who has just spent a decade dismantling the possibility of Roman politics is being told, by a dancer he has already banished once, what the dancers are for. Dio records no reply.
stops.quote: It is to your advantage, Caesar, that the people should devote their spare time to us.
stops.quote_source: Pylades to Augustus, Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.5 (lexundria.com)
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4-5, under the year 18 BCE

stops.name: Rome, the parties in the seats
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Dio attests the quarrel and the emperor's intervention. Organised partisan factions attached specifically to Bathyllus are inferred from the better-documented pantomime rioting of the following generation (Tacitus, Annals 1.54, 1.77, 4.14) and are not stated for the Augustan period.
stops.campa: Something in the seats has to explain why an emperor troubles himself over a squabble between two performers. In the reign after this one the pattern is unmistakable: partisans of rival pantomimes fighting in the theatres, soldiers posted, a praetor killed in the crush, the Senate legislating on where actors may live and who may watch them rehearse. Nothing that violent is recorded while Bathyllus is dancing. What is recorded is a rebuke from Augustus, which means the rivalry had already grown large enough for a government to notice it. The evidence for organised factions is Tacitus's, and it is from 15 and 23 CE, decades later.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 1.77 and 4.14, on theatrical disorder and senatorial restrictions on actors, 15 and 23 CE
sources: Tacitus, Annals 1.54, 1.77, 4.14 (the later disorder, decades after Bathyllus's floruit)

stops.name: Rome, the field cleared by somebody else's punishment
stops.date_confidence: Attested for Pylades and Hylas (Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45), undated in the source. Bathyllus is named nowhere in that chapter; no source shows him present, punished, or benefiting by design. Included as the documented fate of his rival, not as an event in his own life, and the year orders the segment only.
stops.campa: Suetonius lists what Augustus did to dancers. Pylades he expelled from the city and from Italy as well, for pointing a finger at a spectator who was hissing him and turning every eye in the theatre onto the heckler. Hylas he had flogged on a praetor's complaint, in the atrium of Hylas's own house, with nobody shut out. Bathyllus is not in the chapter. Why the punishments fell on one side of the rivalry and not the other is a question Suetonius does not raise, and no other source raises it either.
stops.quote: Pylades was expelled from the city and from Italy as well, because by pointing at him with his finger he turned all eyes upon a spectator who was hissing him.
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45, Rolfe's Loeb translation (penelope.uchicago.edu)
suggested_refs: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45, on Augustus's discipline of the stage

stops.name: Rome, the piper called Princeps
stops.date_confidence: Phaedrus wrote in the first half of the first century CE and the fable is comedy, not reportage. The casual reference to Bathyllus as the piper's former employer is nonetheless evidence of a standing performance partnership. The date orders the segment and documents nothing.
stops.campa: Phaedrus tells it as a joke about vanity. A flute player called Princeps, moderately well known, used to work the stage for Bathyllus. He recovers from a bad fall, returns, and the chorus strikes up its song for the emperor: rejoice, Rome, safe and whole, your Princeps unharmed. The piper takes the acclamation for himself. Behind the joke sits an ordinary working fact: Bathyllus employed stage machinery and musicians, and one of them was known by name outside the theatre. The fall came as the pegma was being hoisted, and what broke was his left tibia, which in Latin is both a shinbone and a pipe.
stops.quote: Princeps tibicen notior paulo fuit, operam Bathyllo solitus in scaena dare.
suggested_refs: Phaedrus, Fabulae 5.7, 'Princeps tibicen,' on the pegma, the broken tibia, and the canticum

stops.name: Rome, the rhetorician's boast
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3 praef. 16, written decades afterward and recalling the declamation halls of the Augustan period. Neither the occasion nor the year of Cestius's remark is given; the setting near the Forum is a plausible placement, not a location named in the text.
stops.campa: Cestius Pius, teaching declamation to the sons of senators, wants the room to know exactly how good he considers himself, and reaches for three names outside his own trade to say it. If I were a Thracian gladiator I would be Fusius; if I were a pantomime I would be Bathyllus; if a horse, Melissio. The comparison only carries if each name is past arguing about. A freedman dancer is doing that work in the sentence, standing between a champion of the arena and a racehorse everybody in Rome has bet on. Seneca the Elder wrote the boast down decades afterward, from memory.
stops.quote: si Thraex essem, Fusius essem; si pantomimus essem, Bathyllus essem; si equus, Melissio.
stops.quote_source: Cestius Pius, in Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3, praefatio 16 (Latin, thelatinlibrary.com)
suggested_refs: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae, prefaces, on the declaimers of the Augustan schools

stops.name: The Esquiline, the death of Maecenas
stops.date_confidence: Maecenas's death in 8 BCE is securely attested. His burial on the far Esquiline, near where Horace was buried weeks later, comes from Suetonius, Vita Horati: sepulti sunt ambo extremis Esquiliis iuxta Maecenatis tumulum. Nothing places Bathyllus at the death, in the will, or anywhere in the accounts of either.
stops.campa: Maecenas dies in 8 BCE and is buried on the far Esquiline, where Horace will be laid beside him within weeks. The gardens pass to the emperor. Everything Bathyllus's position rested on ends inside that single year: the household, the patronage, the man. He is by then about sixty, if the modern guess at his birth is anywhere near right, and has been a freedman for perhaps twenty years. No source records whether he was present at the death, was named in the will, was provided for, or was already dead himself.
suggested_refs: Suetonius, Vita Horati, on the tombs of Horace and Maecenas on the far Esquiline
sources: Standard chronology of Maecenas's death, 8 BCE
Absence of any Bathyllus mention in surviving accounts of it

stops.name: Rome, the last sighting that may not be one
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Crinagoras epigram cannot be securely dated within Augustus's reign, so it may be either an early or a late witness. Placed here to register that it might be the last live sighting; nothing supports that position except the impossibility of ruling it out.
stops.campa: The Crinagoras epigram floats loose in the reign. It could belong to the twenties, when the form was new, or to the last years of Augustus, when Bathyllus would be an old man still working. Nothing inside the poem fixes a year and nothing outside it does either. If it is late, then the last surviving sentence about a living Bathyllus is a friendly note to a librettist about a piece not yet written, promising that the dancer's hands will not let him down. If it is early, then the following two or three decades produced not one line that anybody kept.
suggested_refs: Modern discussion of the dating of Crinagoras's corpus within the Augustan period
sources: Crinagoras, Greek Anthology 9.542; dating uncertainty noted in the modern literature on his corpus

stops.name: Rome, the record simply stops
stops.date_confidence: Attested only as an absence. No source records a retirement, a final performance, an illness, a death date, a cause, a will, a tomb, a marriage, or children. The date is an arbitrary marker for the end of attestation and documents nothing whatever.
stops.campa: There is no death scene. No ancient writer records when Bathyllus stopped dancing, where he went, what he owned, whom he left it to, or where he was buried. He is not in the Augustal Games of 14 CE, when the actors' rivalry finally turns into open disorder. He is not named in the Senate's debates on actors in 15 or 23. He is in no list of the emperor's household and no register of the professional associations. There is no grave, no bust, no inscription. Latin writers go on using his name as a unit of measurement for two more centuries.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 1.54, on the disorder at the first Augustal Games, 14 CE, where Bathyllus is not named
sources: Absence across Tacitus, Suetonius, Cassius Dio, both Senecas, Persius, Phaedrus, Crinagoras
Wikipedia, 'Bathyllus,' which likewise reports no burial or portrait record

stops.name: Rome, nothing under his own name
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an absence and cross-checked against the testimonia compilations and general reference works, which likewise report no tomb, portrait, or authored text. The treatise Peri orcheseos belongs to Pylades on Athenaeus's own attribution. The date is a marker only.
stops.campa: Pylades leaves a book. Athenaeus says so directly, and the treatise on dancing is credited to him by name. Bathyllus leaves nothing: no letter, no notation, no inscription he paid for, no epitaph, no securely identified likeness in stone or paint. What exists of him is entirely other people's sentences about him, and most of those were written after his death by men who had never watched him move. Athenaeus, the fullest of them, was working around 200 CE from Seleucus and Aristonicus, whose own books are lost too.
suggested_refs: Athenaeus's attribution of the lost Peri orcheseos to Pylades, not to Bathyllus

segments.name: The House That Stands Through Successors

stops.name: Rome, still the measure, two generations on
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Seneca the Elder compiled the Controversiae in the 30s CE, under Tiberius or Caligula, recalling declamation from decades earlier; he was dead by about 39. The date is approximate to the composition and marks no event in Bathyllus's life.
stops.campa: Seneca the Elder is an old man writing down what he heard in the halls of his youth, and Bathyllus is in the material twice: once as the benchmark Cestius invokes, once as half of the pair that proves a specialist should stay in his own register. Neither passage explains who Bathyllus was. The compiler assumes his readers know, the way one assumes a reader knows what a consul is. He put the collection together in the 30s CE, for his sons, and was dead by about 39.
suggested_refs: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3, praefatio, sections 10 and 16
sources: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3 praef. 10 and 16 (thelatinlibrary.com)

stops.name: Rome, the house that stands through successors
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Seneca the Younger, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32.3, composed in his retirement between 62 and 64 CE; he was dead by April 65. Evidence for an institution carrying the name, not for Bathyllus being alive.
stops.campa: Seneca the Younger, complaining that philosophy's schools are being allowed to die while nobody lets the entertainers lapse, puts it in a single sentence: the house of Pylades and of Bathyllus stands through successors, and of these arts there are many pupils and many teachers. Eighty years after the Italian dance was assembled, the two names have become the names of institutions, each with a teaching line, a repertoire, and heirs. Whatever a man from Alexandria did with his hands in the twenties BCE is by now a curriculum, and other people are performing it.
stops.quote: Stat per successores Pyladis et Bathylli domus, harum artium multi discipuli sunt multique doctores.
stops.quote_source: Seneca the Younger, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32.3 (Latin, thelatinlibrary.com)
suggested_refs: Seneca the Younger, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32, on the schools that survive and the schools that do not

stops.name: The Circus Flaminius quarter, a second Bathyllus dances Leda
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Juvenal names a Bathyllus dancing Leda (Satires 6.63); the identification with the Alexandrian is chronologically impossible. Satire 6 belongs to Book II, conventionally dated c. 115-127 CE on internal evidence, some 135 years after the 22 BCE horizon. The testimonia collections list this performer separately as Bathyllus II, active under Domitian and Trajan.
stops.campa: Juvenal describes Roman matrons at the theatre, undone while a soft Bathyllus dances a gesturing Leda: Tuccia loses command of herself, Apula moans, Thymele the country girl watches and takes notes. This Bathyllus is not the Alexandrian and cannot be. A century and a third stands between them. The name has been picked up by a later performer, or handed down inside the school, the way a shop keeps its founder's sign over the door long after the founder. The testimonia collections file him separately, as Bathyllus II, active under Domitian and Trajan.
suggested_refs: Aubrey Beardsley, 'Bathyllus in the Swan Dance (Unpublished illustration for The Sixth Satire of Juvenal),' line-block print, about 1896, Hood Museum of Art, Dartmouth, PR.917.12.3, which illustrates this later Bathyllus rather than the Alexandrian
sources: theatrum.de, s.v. Bathyllus II, placing him under Domitian and Trajan

stops.name: Rome, four men and one word
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a problem in the testimonia rather than as an event. The Verona stele of Gaius Silius Bathyllus (inscription IG II-2 5302, now Museo Lapidario Maffei) is a second-century monument to a boy of an Athenian theatrical family, a different person entirely; Bathyllus of Samos, Anacreon's beloved and named by Horace at Epodes 14.9-10, is a sixth-century BCE figure. The date marks the stele, not anything in the Alexandrian's life.
stops.campa: The name will not stay attached to one person. There is the Alexandrian. There is the later dancer Juvenal attacks. There is Gaius Silius Bathyllus, a boy of an Athenian theatrical family whose funerary stele was cut in the second century and now stands in the Museo Lapidario Maffei at Verona. Further back still there is Bathyllus of Samos, whom Anacreon loved five centuries before any of them and whom Horace names in an epode. Modern reference works still fold the Samian's Polycrates into the Alexandrian's biography.
suggested_refs: The funerary stele of Gaius Silius Bathyllus, Museo Lapidario Maffei, Verona (IG II-2 5302)
Horace, Epodes 14.9-10, on Anacreon and Bathyllus of Samos
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bathyllus,' which still attaches Polycrates to the Augustan dancer

stops.name: Rome, everything is somebody else's sentence
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a bibliographic fact. Athenaeus wrote c. 200 CE and preserves the fullest ancient notice, itself quoting the earlier scholars Seleucus and Aristonicus from works now lost. The date marks Athenaeus's composition, not any event.
stops.campa: Count what there is. Two Latin historians writing a century and two centuries afterward, both explaining a patron's appetite. One Greek epigram from his own lifetime, addressed to somebody else. One preface by a rhetorician's father. A satirist's insult, a fabulist's joke, a Stoic's complaint about schools. And Athenaeus, at a banquet of scholars around the year 200, quoting Seleucus and Aristonicus quoting sources already lost by then. That is the entire file. Every sentence in it was written by a man with other business in hand.
suggested_refs: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d-f, and the earlier authorities Seleucus and Aristonicus whom he quotes

stops.name: Alexandria, the adjective outlives the man
stops.date_confidence: Marker only. Athenaeus, himself an Egyptian Greek of Naucratis, is the source of the byname. No ancient text records anything about Bathyllus's relation to Alexandria after he left it, or whether he ever returned; the 1894 novel and the 1890s illustration listed in the refs are modern receptions, staged at their own authors' desks and not events here.
stops.campa: Athenaeus is himself an Egyptian Greek, born at Naucratis on the Nile, and it is he who keeps the byname alive. Not Bathyllus of Rome, where the entire career happened, but Bathyllus of Alexandria. Nothing in the record says he ever went back. No source names an Alexandrian relative, a return voyage, or any claim he made on the city. Whether the word was his own, kept up in Rome as a stage name, or a label a compatriot fixed to him two hundred years after his death, Athenaeus does not say.
suggested_refs: Jean Bertheroy (Berthe-Corinne Le Barillier), Le Mime Bathylle, roman historique (Paris: Armand Colin, 1894)
Aubrey Beardsley, 'Bathyllus in the Swan Dance,' about 1896, Hood Museum of Art, Dartmouth, PR.917.12.3
